The Remainder of the Chapter on the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu:
"Furthermore, the yoga practitioner forms this mental image: "
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas now descend and manifest their majestic power and great supernormal faculties.

Having formed this visualization, one should further contemplate the manner in which Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment—just as the Bodhisattva Śākya, within a distance of one *yojana* near the Bodhi tree, practiced various ascetic disciplines for six full years, vowing to realize the Buddha-way, proceeded to the Bodhi tree, sat upon the Vajra-seat, and entered the Vajra-samādhi.

At that time, the Tathāgata Vairocana, having observed this, proceeded to the Bodhi tree at the Vajra-maṇḍala and manifested countless transformation Buddhas filling the void of space like motes of dust; each with a single voice, they addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!
"What is the method for not seeking to become a Buddha?
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva joined his palms in reverent devotion and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not yet know the method for becoming a Buddha; I only pray that, out of your compassion, you will show me the path to Bodhi."
Then the manifested Buddhas said to the Bodhisattvas:
"Good sons! The mind is bodhi; you should seek it within your own minds."
The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with one voice and in unison, proclaimed the Dharmakāya-cittārthamantra:

"Oṃ śiddha pratividhe dhāni karu mi. At that time, having heard this Dharma, the Bodhisattva bound the Vajrabandha mudrā, interlacing his two hands into fists and placing them at his heart. With single-minded focus, he contemplated the meaning and intent of the mantra and addressed the Buddhas, saying:
"I have attained this Dharma."
Then the Buddha asked, "What kind of dharma have you attained? The Bodhisattva replied, "The mind is bodhi; I have attained this dharma."
The Buddhas said: "Examine and analyze it once more with even greater subtlety.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The mind, consciousness, and the dharmas of the mental sense-field (dharmāyatana) are all afflictions that are mutually blended and harmonized, such that they cannot be distinguished.

Yet, when seeking the mind and mental factors among all phenomena, they are entirely unobtainable; they are unobtainable when sought within the five aggregates (skandhas), unobtainable within the twelve bases (āyatanas), unobtainable within the eighteen elements (dhātus), and even unobtainable within the eighteen kinds of emptiness."

The dharmas of the aggregates, bases, and elements are each individually analyzed: the essence of all dharmas is devoid of self and what belongs to a self; the person (pudgala) is devoid of self and what belongs to a self. The mind and mental factors are originally without birth and have no place of cessation; they cannot be seen within any of the minds of the world. They are non-existent internally, non-existent externally, and non-existent in between. A past mind cannot be apprehended, a present mind cannot be apprehended, and a future mind cannot be apprehended; they are like magical illusions, without any distinction.
"I have now personally realized that all things are exactly thus.
World-Honored One!
According to my understanding, the mind and mental factors are originally empty and quiescent; by means of what dharma could one seek to attain the path of Buddhahood?"
The Buddhas replied:

"When the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are in conjunction, one spontaneously experiences suffering and pleasure; this is called 'self-awakened mind. It is that which only oneself can perceive and which others do not awaken to; based upon this mind, the bodhicitta is established."

"Furthermore, after the yoga practitioner has observed the mind as that bodhisattva did, he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), performs the *vajrabandha* mudrā, places it against his heart, closes both eyes, and intently observes his own mind. He practices the mantra for seeking the mind with his mouth and contemplates the meaning of the secret [mantra] with his mind."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The practitioner visualizes the lunar disk, And within meditative concentration, universally prostrates at the feet [of the Buddhas], saying:
‘I only pray that all Tathāgatas Will show me the place where I should practice.’”
The Buddhas spoke with one voice:
"You should contemplate your own mind.
Having heard these words, he observed in accordance with the instruction.
Dwelling for a long time in profound contemplation, he did not perceive the marks of his own mind;
he then further visualized prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“O Most Victorious Honored One!”
"I do not perceive my own mind; what are the characteristics of this mind?
All the Buddhas replied in unison:
"The characteristics of the mind are difficult to fathom; we grant you the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra). Examine it with truth according to the principle."
"Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga binds the Vajrabandha mudrā, performs the visualization of the aspect of the bodhicitta, and practices the mantra.
Then all these emanation Buddhas say to the Bodhisattva:
'O Son of Good Family!'"
"You should generate the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What is called the mind of great bodhicitta?"
The Buddhas replied:

"Immeasurable wisdom is like a mote of dust, accomplished through diligent cultivation for one hundred kalpas within three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. It is far removed from all afflictions and faults, and it accomplishes merit and wisdom as vast as space. That which can produce such a most supreme and wondrous fruit is precisely the unsurpassed Great Bodhicitta."
For example, among the human body, the mind is foremost;
likewise, the great bodhicitta is the most supreme within the triple-thousandfold world system.
For what reason is it called "foremost"?
"It means that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are born from the bodhicitta.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What are the characteristics of the Great Bodhicitta?"
The Buddhas replied:
"For example, it is like the full orb of the moon spanning fifty yojanas—cool, bright, and pure, free from all clouds and veils; you should know that this is the characteristic of the bodhicitta."
Having spoken these words, immeasurable Buddhas, with one voice and in unison, proclaimed the mantra of the Great Bodhicitta, saying:
“Oṃ muni śodhani bodhye mi. Just as that Bodhisattva contemplates the Bodhicitta, so too should the practitioner of yoga do likewise.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke in verse:
"In a single thought-moment, one perceives the pure mind, Perfect and full like the autumn moon;
Then one reflects further:"
"What is this mind? It is the seeds of the habitual tendencies of afflictions. Good and evil both arise from the mind;
the mind is the *ālaya*, serving as the foundation for pure consciousness."
Because it is perfumed by the six perfections, that mind becomes the Great Mind.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is fundamentally not defiled; it is pure and free from blemish.
Having cultivated merit and wisdom since beginningless time, it is like the pure, full moon.
It has neither substance nor function; it is the moon, yet not the moon.
Because it is endowed with merit and wisdom, the full moon is like one's own mind.
The Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with joy, and he again addressed the Buddhas, saying:
“I have now perceived the nature of the mind; it is as pure as the lunar disc, free from the stains of all afflictions, and devoid of both the grasper and the grasped.”
All the Buddhas spoke in unison:
"The nature of your mind has always been thus; it is merely obscured by adventitious defilements, and so you have not awakened to the bodhicitta."
“Observe the pure lunar disc, contemplating it in every thought-moment;
this can cause wisdom to become manifest and lead to the realization of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, the yoga practitioner binds the vajra-bond mudrā, relying on the previous contemplation and practicing the mantra, just as the emanated Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva:
“Good son! Furthermore, there is the mantra of the firm bodhicitta, which says:
‘Oṃ niṣṭhā vajra. At that time, the Bodhisattva, relying on his previous contemplation, addressed the Buddha, saying:”
“I have now seen it.
The Buddha said,
“In what way have you seen it?”
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I see five-pronged vajras within the full moon, by which all afflictions are utterly shattered and pulverized;
like refined gold, their color is brilliantly radiant."
"Such wisdom is the most supreme; it is the adamantine body of all Buddhas, neither born nor extinguished.
Just as that Bodhisattva contemplates the lunar disc, so too does the practitioner of yoga.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga contemplates his own body as Vajrasattva, and while forming the mudrā and reciting the hundred-syllable mantra, he realizes that Vajrasattva is indeed the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Tathāgata Vairocana."
As the various emanation Buddhas said to the Bodhisattvas:
"O sons of noble family!
There is furthermore a mantra like a vajra, which says: [mantra]"
"Oṃ vāru-dharma-gu hūṃ (with a loud sound). At that time, the Bodhisattva, relying on his previous contemplation, addressed the Buddhas, saying:
"I have now seen it."
The Buddha asked,
"In what way have you seen it? He replied:

"I have now become Vajrasattva; upon my head is a jeweled crown with five transformation Buddhas, and in my hand I hold a vajra as the Lord of Dharma, to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings."
"Just as that Bodhisattva contemplates Vajrasattva, so too does the yoga practitioner: with eyes closed and sitting upright, they form this thought:

'My own body is Vajrasattva; upon my head is a jeweled crown, within which the transformation Buddhas of the five directions sit in the full lotus posture, their right hands holding vajra-clubs against the lower part of their right chests.'"
"If one raises this mallet, it can immediately destroy all heavy obscurations and afflictions within all sentient beings and within oneself.
Having performed this visualization, one should bind the Vajrabandha mudrā and recite this mantra.

"Furthermore, the yoga practitioner next visualizes the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the five directions, along with their retinues, entering into his own body. Just as the emanation-Buddhas address the Bodhisattvas, saying:
'O Son of Good Family!'"
There is a mantra identical to that of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, which says:
"Oṃ yathā-sarvadharmāḥ svabhāva-śuddhās tathā-hūṃ. At that time, the Bodhisattva, observing according to his previous method, said:
"I have seen it."
"How do you see them? he asked. He replied:

"The Buddhas of the three periods of time and their retinues, as well as bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms and countless devas and nāgas, enter and exit my body from the worlds of the ten directions, appearing in the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated."
"These five directional Buddhas enter my body; possessing the three realities, they collectively constitute my own essence. That which all Buddhas realize is solely this Dharmakāya.

Just as that bodhisattva visualizes the Buddhas and others entering his body, so too does the yoga practitioner: sitting upright with eyes closed and forming the vajra-bond mudrā, he forms this thought:
"The Buddhas of the five directions and all the bodhisattvas, each leading their countless retinues and celestial music, enter my body. As for the bodies of those Buddhas:"
First, white; second, blue; third, golden; fourth, red; fifth, variegated.
Furthermore, one should form this thought:
"The wondrous fruits of the three bodies and the three realities are all fully perfected within my own body.
In this manner, one should constantly observe them in every moment of thought.
Having performed this visualization, one practices that mantra and further reflects:

"Such a gate of contemplation is the realm of the Buddhas; I have now for the first time awakened to the purity of my own mind, seeing my body as a Buddha with all marks perfected, thereby attaining bodhi."
Within that meditative concentration, he universally pays homage to all Buddhas, vowing that they will bestow their protection so that he may realize the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga performs the visualization of the Saṃbhogakāya, just as the various Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas address the Bodhisattvas, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
There is a *saṃbhogakāya* mantra, which says:
"Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham. At that time, the Bodhisattva, observing according to the previous [instruction], said:
"I have now seen it."
The Buddha asked, "How do you see it? He replied:

“Dharma and non-Dharma are by nature pure; they are like a lotus flower that, though born from within the mud, remains unstained by dust. My present contemplation of this is precisely the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya).”

Just as that Bodhisattva performs the contemplation of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), so too should the practitioner of yoga: sitting upright with a settled mind, forming the Vajra-Bandhaka mudrā, one should form this thought:
"Dharma and non-Dharma are fundamentally pure, like a lotus flower; though it grows from within the mud, dust cannot defile it.
The Reward Bodies of all Buddhas and my own Reward Body are likewise; although they appear to enjoy clothing, food, drink, and the music of the devas, the mind is not stained by attachment."
Having formed this thought, one practices its mantra.
Furthermore, the yoga practitioner performs the visualization of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), just as the various emanation Buddhas address the Bodhisattvas, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
There is a transformation-body mantra, which says:
"Oṃ sarvathā svāhā hūṃ. At that time, the Bodhisattva, observing according to his previous visualization, addressed the Buddhas, saying:
"I have now seen it."
The Buddha asked, "How do you see it? He replied:

"Endowed with various marks and characteristics, this person possesses the Noble Path; whether manifesting transformation bodies for each individual sentient being, or observing all sentient beings each becoming a Buddha—now I perceive this as a transformation body."
At that time, having heard this mantra, the Bodhisattva immediately realized and attained the wondrous fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Just as that Bodhisattva performed the visualization of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), so too should the yoga practitioner: sitting upright with right mindfulness, forming the *vajrabandha* mudrā, they should form this mental image:

"I now possess various names and various physical forms: sometimes descending from Tuṣita Heaven into a mother’s womb; sometimes achieving full lifespan with the six sense faculties complete; sometimes appearing like the sun or moon; sometimes sitting beneath the Bodhi tree; sometimes subduing the four kinds of māra armies; sometimes turning the wheel of Dharma at the request of Brahmā Devarāja to deliver all sentient beings; sometimes engaging in debate to defeat the various non-Buddhists; sometimes descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by the triple-staged jeweled staircase; sometimes manifesting the Vajrakrodha Bodhisattva Maheśvara-vijaya Great Maṇḍala to subdue Māra, Maheśvara, and all evil spirits and deities; or, having completed the work of teaching and transforming, entering the peerless and tranquil Dharma-realm."
The practitioner of yoga should likewise do so; having visualized their own body in this manner, they should hold this mantra.
Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga should form the Vajrabandha mudrā and form this thought:
"Just as the space of the worlds of the ten directions is inexhaustible, so too do I perceive the three bodies and the three realities to be firm, permanent, and eternally abiding."
For the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one should constantly perform such sublime contemplation day and night.
Having performed this contemplation, one should hold the mantra, saying:

“Oṃ sarvadharmatā-viśvamantrodita vajra tiṣṭha. Furthermore, the yoga practitioner forms the seal of perfection (*paripūrṇa-mudrā*): with the palms facing upward, he presses the thumb over the little finger of the right hand, while the remaining three fingers stand erect. Holding water in his palms, he consecrates it seven times; first, he sprinkles one portion upon his crown, next, he drinks one portion, and finally, he scatters one portion in the four directions.
After scattering [the flowers], one should form this thought:
"My body is as firm and solid as a vajra, and all sentient beings shall likewise attain long life.

If one empowers water with this seal and mantra and sprinkles it upon all objects of offering and the like, they will all become auspicious and supremely pure; the Vināyakas and various malevolent spirits will be unable to defile them, nor will they find any opportunity to do so.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vāruḍaka ṭa. What benefit does the practitioner of yoga obtain by observing in this manner, day and night?
That is to say, by relying on such and such contemplation, one swiftly gains entry into the secret realm of all Buddhas.
When a practitioner of yoga cultivates this contemplation, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly provide protection, and whatever aspirations they hold in their hearts shall all be fulfilled.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas came to him and, snapping their fingers as before, addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
"O virtuous woman!

Diligently apply your efforts to cultivate this Dharma-gate; then, the most supreme and excellent fruits of all worlds will be attained spontaneously without being sought, and you shall swiftly realize Bodhi in a future life."

"Furthermore, the practitioner of yoga enters the Samādhi of Vairocana; sitting upright with the body straight, he must not allow himself to waver. He places his tongue against the upper palate and fixes his mind on the tip of the nose. He visualizes for himself a celestial crown of five jewels upon his head, within which five transformation Buddhas sit in the full lotus posture."

Having performed this visualization, one should immediately form the firm Vajra-fist mudrā: first, insert the left and right thumbs respectively into the palms of the left and right hands; then, firmly clench the remaining four fingers of both hands to form fists. This is the firm Vajra-fist mudrā.

Next, extend the left index finger and place the back of the left fist against the heart, with the palm turned toward the left side. Then, grasp the first joint of the left index finger with the little finger of the right fist, and touch the tip of the right index finger to the first joint of the right thumb, also placing it before the heart. This is called the First Wisdom Seal of the Guide to Bodhi, and is also called the Seal that Can Extinguish the Darkness of Ignorance.

Through the empowerment of this seal, all Buddhas bestow upon the practitioner the supreme and definitive prophecy of unsurpassed bodhi; it is the Great Seal of Wondrous Wisdom of the Tathāgata Vairocana.

Once the practitioner of yoga has bound this mudrā, they should direct their mind to visualize that all sentient beings likewise bind this mudrā; that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the three evil realms and the karmic fruits of the eight difficulties no longer exist, and that all beings enjoy the bliss of the ultimate truth.
The mantra is: Oṃ hūṃ jaḥ eḥ saḥ. Furthermore, the yoga practitioner, while holding this mantra, should observe the color and form of each of these five syllables one by one.
"First, bind the Bodhi-mudrā.
Entering the samādhi of Vairocana Tathāgata, one should contemplate that the color of the syllable 'Oṃ' (𑆃), as well as my own body and the worlds of the ten directions, are all entirely white."

When a practitioner of yoga cultivates this gate of contemplation, all ignorance, afflictions, and evil karma belonging to themselves and all sentient beings will naturally be extinguished, so that the practitioner and all sentient beings may swiftly attain Buddhahood.
"Second, bind the seal that destroys Māra.

Extend the five fingers of the right hand to press upon the earth, and with the five fingers of the left hand, grasp the corner of the robe. Enter the Samādhi of the Tathāgata Acala of the East; one should contemplate that the color of the syllable ‘HŪṂ’ and my own body, extending throughout the eastern realm and all the infinite worlds of the nine directions—including all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—are entirely blue in color, while the palm of the right hand presses down upon the earth."
This mudrā can cause all māras, yakṣas, and all afflictions to remain utterly unmoved; it is called the Mudrā for Extinguishing Vināyakas and All Evil Māras and Yakṣas.
"Third, bind the seal for fulfilling all vows.

With the left hand as before, extend the five fingers of the right hand with the palm facing upward; enter the samādhi of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava of the south. One should contemplate that the color of the syllable 𑖮𑖿 (Ja), my own body, the entirety of the southern world, and all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, sentient beings, herbs, trees, mountains, and rivers throughout the infinite worlds of the nine directions are all the color of yellow gold."

Immediately forming this thought, he causes wish-fulfilling jewels to rain down from between his five fingers. These wish-fulfilling jewels rain down celestial garments, celestial sublime nectar, celestial sublime music, and celestial jewel palaces; even unto all that sentient beings desire, they cause it all to be fulfilled. This seal is named "The Seal Capable of Fulfilling All That Sentient Beings Love and Delight In," for it is able to fulfill every aspiration of sentient beings.
"Fourth, the mudrā for binding and removing the distracted mind:
First, extend the five fingers of the left hand and place them before the navel wheel; next, extend the five fingers of the right hand and place them upon the palm of the left hand."

Having bound this mudrā, one enters the samādhi of the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the western quarter. One should contemplate that the color of the syllable *Ē* (𑀕), as well as my own body and the entirety of the western realm—including all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the infinite worlds in the nine directions, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—are entirely the color of red lotuses. This is because it enables the practitioner and all sentient beings to eliminate distracted minds and enter samādhi.
"Fifth, form the Seal of Fearlessness.

With the left hand as before, extend the five fingers of the right hand with the palm facing outward. Enter the samādhi of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the North; one should contemplate that the color of the syllable 'ZA' (佐), my own body, the entirety of the northern realm, as well as the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, and forests of the infinite worlds of the nine directions, are all of five colors."
By what causes and conditions is he named "Fearless"?
It is because he is endowed with four meanings that he is called Fearless:

first, the Tathāgata Vairocana of the Central Region is able to extinguish the darkness of ignorance and give birth to the *prajñāpāramitā*... and so forth, such that his penetrating radiance fills the entire realm of empty space.
Second, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the east can subdue all pināyakas, evil māras, ghosts, spirits, and the like, rendering them entirely motionless.

Third, the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava of the south can eliminate poverty and bestow celestial palaces, celestial food and drink, celestial garments, and celestial music, all of which are perfectly fulfilled.

Fourth, the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the west can grant the practitioner the great bliss of samādhi; just as the space of the ten directions is immeasurable and inexhaustible, just as sentient beings are immeasurable and inexhaustible, and just as afflictions are immeasurable and inexhaustible, so too is the great bliss of samādhi for the yoga practitioner immeasurable and inexhaustible.
Since these four meanings are thus fully and perfectly complete, the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the northern direction addresses the practitioner, saying:
"O son of good family! O daughter of good family!"
"Do not be afraid.
For this reason, it is called the "Seal of Fearlessness.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"I have now explained the mudrās and mantras of the five Buddhas; next, I shall explain the mudrās and mantras of the four Pāramitā goddesses.
Furthermore, regarding the Vajrapāramitā goddess in the northeast corner, who belongs to Akṣobhya Tathāgata: her mudrā and visualization are identical to those of Akṣobhya Tathāgata."
The practitioner forms the mudrā and recites the mantra:

"Oṃ saptavajri. Furthermore, at the southeast corner is the deity Ratnapāramitā, who belongs to the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava; her mudrā, visualization, and contemplation are all like those of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava.
The practitioner forms the mudrā and recites the mantra:

"Oṃ ratna vajri. Furthermore, at the southwest corner is the Dharma-pāramitā-devī, who belongs to Amitāyus Tathāgata; her mudrā, visualization, and contemplation are all identical to those of Amitāyus Tathāgata.
The practitioner forms the mudrā and recites the mantra:

"Oṃ dharmadhātu-vajri. Furthermore, in the northwest corner is the deity of the Karma-pāramitā, who belongs to Akṣobhya Tathāgata; the visualization of the mudrā and the contemplation are both identical to those of Akṣobhya Tathāgata.
The practitioner forms the mudrā and recites the mantra: "Oṃ karoma vajri. Furthermore, Vajrapāṇi!

I have now explained the methods of internal offering, all of which involve visualizations of the moon disk and other such signs. Next, I shall expound upon the sublime visualization of signlessness (*animitta*).

The yoga practitioner, sitting upright and practicing correct contemplation, should clearly visualize the moon disk and form various mudrās. [One should contemplate] the singing and dancing, the burning of incense, the application of fragrant ointments, flower garlands, gardens, groves, cities, towns, villages, rivers, oceans, the Snowy Mountains, the Black Mountains, the sun, moon, and constellations, kings, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, spiritual friends, and retinues, up to and including bodhisattvas of the ten stages, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the ten wholesome actions, and the six perfections (*pāramitā*)... all such numerical characteristics and even down to a single atom are entirely empty and quiescent.

If you see such signs and appearances even in a dream, do not rejoice; even if you see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions appearing before you, do not rejoice. Rather, seek only the fruit of Buddhahood with single-mindedness, maintaining non-conceptual contemplation, standing firm and unmoving like Mount Sumeru, and remaining far removed from all deluded thoughts and discriminations.
"If a practitioner of yoga has not attained siddhi, they should contemplate the forms and characteristics of the thirty-seven deities;
if they have realized siddhi, they do not grasp at these forms, but instead establish the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
If one contemplates the form of bodhicitta as being like the orb of the moon, crystal, or the color of milk—such characteristics are all objects of contemplation for ordinary beings."

"If an ordinary person cultivates this gate of contemplation, even though they have committed the five heinous crimes or the extremely grave evil karma of an icchantika, it will all be completely extinguished, and they shall immediately obtain five kinds of samādhis:

first, the samādhi of a single instant; second, the samādhi of a mote of dust; third, the samādhi of white threads; fourth, the samādhi of concealment and manifestation; and fifth, the samādhi of peaceful abiding."

"O Vajrapāṇi! I have now already taught the mantras and mudrās of the five directional Tathāgatas and the four Pāramitās, as well as the individual mantras and mudrās of Vajrasattva and the others; I shall now teach you the sequence of the seating order."

Chapter Four: The External Realm of Vajra. From the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*, the Scripture on the Compendium of the Real Sphere of All Buddhas. Chapter Four: The External Realm of Vajra. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I only pray that you will speak of it; I only pray that you will speak of it. I am deeply thirsty for it and yearn to hear it.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

However, regarding the methods of these mudrās, there are distinctions in their names: the Tathāgatas of the five directions, the four pāramitās, and the sixteen bodhisattvas all receive the designation "mudrā";
whereas although other ritual gestures (mudrā-dharma) also receive the name "mudrā," they differ in meaning.
What is their differentiation?

The five directional Buddhas, the four pāramitās, and the sixteen bodhisattvas are called the *tathatāmudrā* (True Seal); Vajralāsyā and others are called the *pratibimbamudrā* (Image Seal); Vajradhūpā and others are called the *upāyamudrā* (Approach Seal); and the Vajrāṅkuśa and others are called the *jñānamudrā* (Wisdom Seal).
For this reason, there is a specific designation:

"The practitioner of yoga who makes offerings to the Tathāgata Vairocana—their own Honored One—by means of the seals (mudrā) and mantras of body, speech, and mind, performs the foremost among all offerings."

"Furthermore, arising from the Karma-pāramitā-samādhi at the northwest corner, one should contemplate the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and the four great Bodhisattvas in the east through the correct contemplation of the Vajrasattva-samādhi;
their names are: the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja, the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga, and the Bodhisattva Vajrasādhu."
The Tathāgata Vairocana sits in the center, facing the east;
the Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the east faces the west, and the four great bodhisattvas are likewise situated.
"Furthermore, one correctly contemplates Vajrasattva Bodhisattva.
The practitioner of yoga visualizes himself:

'My body is Vajrasattva; my speech is Vajra; my mind is Vajra. The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, valleys, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are all entirely blue. "

Having performed this visualization, he immediately formed a vajra-fist with his right hand, placing the thumb inside the palm and firmly grasping it with the remaining four fingers, resting it against his heart.
Next, form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it upon the left hip; this is called the Vajra-Non-Retrogression Mudrā.
Having bound this mudrā, form this mental visualization:
"Until I have attained Buddhahood, I shall never again fall back, and I shall reverently make offerings to the Tathāgata Vairocana."

"By this, one immediately attains the Vajra-Indestructible and Non-retrogressive Samādhi, binds the seal of non-retrogression (Avivartana-mudrā), and recites the mantra: Oṃ vajratāta. Furthermore, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrarāja."
The yoga practitioner visualizes:

"I am the Vajra King; the color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, lands, grasses, trees, ponds, and streams throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are entirely blue."

Having performed this visualization, next one should form the hand-seal (*mudrā*): make both hands into vajra-fists, extend the two index fingers to form a curved hook, and hold them upright with palms facing upward. Then, join the backs of the middle, ring, and little fingers of the two fists together, and place them upright upon the heart.
One should form this thought:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas draw me forth with a hook.
This is what is called the Vajra Hook King.
Having formed this seal-mudrā, recite the mantra: “Oṃ vajrarāja. Next, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga.
The yoga practitioner visualizes: "I am Vajrarāga;

the color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, valleys, ponds, lands, soil, grasses, and trees throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are entirely blue."
Having performed this visualization, one next forms the mudrā.

With both hands, form vajra-fists; imagine the left fist holding a bow and the right fist grasping an arrow. With eyes of compassion, shoot all Māras and all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion. This mudrā is called the "Mudrā for Extirpating Hatred."
For what reason is it called Vajra-love?
It is because this bodhisattva is able to bestow that which practitioners love and delight in.
To form this seal-mudrā, recite the mantra as follows:
“Oṃ vajrarāga. Furthermore, one visualizes the Bodhisattva Vajrasādhu.
The practitioner visualizes:

"I am the Vajra-Sādhu. The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are entirely blue."
Having performed this visualization, one next forms the mudrā.
With both hands, form vajra-fists; first place the left fist upon the right breast, and then place the right fist upon the left breast—this represents the two dharmas of concentration and wisdom.
Crossing the arms at the chest with the vajra-fists represents the power of diligence.
Then, extend the thumbs and index fingers of both hands and snap them three times; this is the gesture of joy.
If one binds this seal, one will immediately attain liberation from the city of ignorance.
Having bound this mudrā, recite the mantra: "Oṃ vajra-sanu.

Furthermore, having first contemplated the Bodhisattva Vajrasādhu from the east, one should enter the gate of the Vajraratna contemplation in the south; that is, one should contemplate the four great Bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava in the south, whose names are:
Vajraratna Bodhisattva, Vajratejas Bodhisattva, Vajraketu Bodhisattva, and Vajrahāsa Bodhisattva.
The Tathāgata Ratnasambhava faces north, and the four great Bodhisattvas do likewise.
The practitioner visualizes:

"I am Vajraratna; the color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees of the worlds of the ten directions, are all golden in color."
Having performed this visualization, one next forms the mudrā.
With both hands, form vajra-fists and place the backs of the two fists upon the two shoulders. Then, form this thought:
"Now I, together with all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sentient beings, receive the empowerment."
Having bound this seal-mudrā, recite the mantra: Oṃ vajraratna. Next, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajratejas.
The practitioner visualizes themselves as the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva), thinking: "In a single kṣaṇa, I am able to completely extinguish all internal and external darkness of all sentient beings."

The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are all the color of gold.
Having formed this visualization, next one should bind the mudrā of the seal.

Forming vajra-fists with both hands, place these two fists side by side upon the heart; then rotate the left and right fists alternately, turning to the right like the sun. One should perform these three rotations because they constitute the wheel of light of the Sun Deity.
Form this mudrā and recite the mantra:
"Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa. Next, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
The practitioner visualizes:
"My body is the Vajradhvaja; rains of all things beloved by sentient beings fall upon my side.
The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees of the worlds of the ten directions, are all golden in color."
Having performed this visualization, one next forms the ritual mudrā.

First, form vajra-fists with both hands, holding the fists facing the practitioner's face. With the two fists held upright in the air to the left and right, it is called the Vajradhvaja-mudrā (Vajra Banner Mudrā), because it can bring to fulfillment all cherished objects of sentient beings.
Form this mudrā and recite the mantra:
"Oṃ vajra-kīrti. Next, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrahāsya.
The practitioner visualizes:

"My body is the Vajra-laughter; the color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees of the worlds of the ten directions, are all golden in color."

Having performed this visualization, one next binds the ritual seal (*mudrā*): with both hands forming vajra-fists, place them at the left and right sides of the mouth and smile three times—first placing the backs of the fists at the left and right sides of the mouth while smiling, then placing the palms of the fists at the left and right sides of the mouth while smiling, and finally placing the backs of the fists at the left and right sides of the mouth while smiling. By doing so, one can cause all sentient beings of the ten directions to attain joy and receive great peace and happiness.
Having bound this mudrā, recite the mantra:

Oṃ vajra hāḥ sā. Furthermore, arising from the gate of contemplation of the Bodhisattva Vajrahāsa in the south, one should enter the gate of contemplation of the Vajradharma in the west; that is to say, contemplate Amitāyus Buddha in the west facing east, and the four great bodhisattvas likewise.
The practitioner visualizes to himself:

"I am the Vajradharma Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees of the worlds of the ten directions, are all the color of red lotuses."
Having formed this visualization, next one should bind the seal of commitment (*samaya-mudrā*).
With both hands in upward-facing vajra-fists, first place the right fist upon the left fist and rotate it once to the right;
then place the left fist upon the right fist and likewise rotate it once.
Again, place the right fist upon the left fist and rotate it once more.
This Vajrapadma-mudrā enables sentient beings to cultivate weary detachment from the world, enter the supramundane Dharma, and enter the City of Nectar.
The mantra is recited as:
Oṃ vajradharmaruṣa. Furthermore, one visualizes the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Sharp Vajra.
The practitioner visualizes:
"I am the true vajra-weapon; I am able to sever the greed, hatred, and delusion of all sentient beings.

My own body, as well as all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests of the worlds of the ten directions, are all the color of red lotuses."
Having performed this visualization, he extends his right fist and immediately forms this thought:
"I now hold a great, sharp sword in my right hand, capable of severing all afflictions of sentient beings."
The mantra is: Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa. Next, one visualizes the Bodhisattva Vajrahetu.
The practitioner forms this thought:
"I am the vajra cause; I am the world’s supreme essence and nectar of immortality; I am the Dharma wheel of the great Vajra teaching."

The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are all the color of red lotuses.

Having formed this thought, one binds the vajra-fists and places the faces of both fists together upon the heart. The middle joints of the middle fingers of both hands touch one another, and they are rotated back and forth three times. Then, one forms this mental visualization:
"I now turn the Vajradharmacakra three times throughout the realms of the ten directions."
The mantra is: Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa. Next, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrabhāṣa.
The practitioner forms this visualization:

"I am the adamantine speech; I am now able to bestow the Susiddhi-dharmas upon all sentient beings. The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, valleys, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests throughout the worlds of the ten directions, are all the color of red lotuses."

Having formed this visualization, place the vajra-fists at the left and right sides of the mouth, making the gesture of coming and going while further adding speech; by binding this seal, one can master the languages of all sentient beings.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajramaśa.

Furthermore, having contemplated from the west the Bodhisattva Vajrabhāṣa, one should enter the gate of contemplation of Vajrakarma in the north. This refers to contemplating the four great Bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi in the north, whose names are:
Vajrakarma Bodhisattva, Vajrarakṣa Bodhisattva, Vajrayakṣa Bodhisattva, and Vajramuṣṭi Bodhisattva.
The practitioner forms this visualization: "I am Vajrakarma;

I am Vajra-amogha, whose fruit is certainly attained—this is the meaning of 'amogha' (unfailing); I am the one who can accomplish all various activities; I am the one who can reach all places; I am the one who can perform all manner of deeds; I am the one who can accomplish sublime undertakings. The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, ponds, grasses, trees, and forests of the worlds of the ten directions, are entirely five colors."
Having formed this thought, one binds the vajra-fist and performs the dance three times; this is called the Seal of Various Activities.
Why is this so? Because it is capable of accomplishing various activities.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajrakarmā. Next, one visualizes the Bodhisattva Vajrarakṣa.
The practitioner forms this thought:
"I am Vajrapāla; I am Vajravarman, firm, solid, and indestructible; I am Vajravīrya;
I am the protector of all immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions, bestowing upon them freedom from fear."

The color of my own body, as well as that of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings, and the mountains, rivers, springs, grasses, trees, and forests of the worlds of the ten directions, are all entirely five colors.

Having formed this visualization, one binds the vajra-fist, extends the two index fingers and places them at the navel; then, separating the fists to both sides, they reach the back, and from the back they return to the navel-cakra. The tips of the two index fingers revolve around each other once; forming this visualization oneself is the meaning of "binding."

Next, place the two index fingers as before at the heart; draw them back to the spine, then return them to the chest, and rotate the tips of the two fingers around each other once. Form this mental visualization yourself; it also carries the meaning of binding.
Next, one proceeds to the neck in the same manner; one forms this mental image as if it were being bound.
The mantra is recited as follows: "Oṃ vajra-rakṣa. Furthermore, one visualizes the Bodhisattva Vajrayakṣa.
The practitioner forms this visualization:
"I am a Vajra Yakṣa, which is the miraculous transformation through the great power of skillful means and supernatural faculties of all Buddhas.
Within my mouth are sharp vajra fangs; all who see me conceive great terror, and I am well able to utterly destroy all demonic adversaries."
"My body is five colors, and all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the worlds of the ten directions are likewise five colors.

Having formed this visualization, one binds the Vajra Fist Mudrā: hooking the left and right little fingers together at the mouth, and extending the two index fingers to rest upon the left and right cheeks; these are the two fangs.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajrajikṣa. Furthermore, one should visualize the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi.
The practitioner forms this thought:
"I am the Vajra Fist; I am able to manifest before all sentient beings; I am the one who can liberate others from the vajra bonds."
"The color of my body, as well as that of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings, and the worlds of the ten directions, are likewise five colors.

Having formed this visualization, one should bind the Seal of the True Vajra Fist: interlace the little fingers of the left and right hands with one another, join the surfaces of the two fists, and grasp firmly without loosening; this is the Seal of the True Vajra Fist.
The mantra is recited as:
"Oṃ vajrasanni. *The Compendium of the Real Sphere of All Buddhas*, Middle Fascicle.
*The Compendium of the Real Sphere of All Buddhas*, Lower Fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīr by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: The Outer Offerings of the Vajradhātu.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:

"I have now explained the five Buddhas Tathāgatas, the four Pāramitās, the sixteen Great Bodhisattvas of the four directions, and the methods for the twenty-five mudrās and mantras. Next, I shall expound the outer court offerings of the twelve Bodhisattvas, such as Vajralāsyā, which benefit and bring peace and happiness to those who seek the Buddha-way, enabling them to attain siddhi in the present life and realize Bodhi in the future."

Furthermore, the yoga practitioner, arising from the visualization gate of the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi to the north, enters the visualization gate of the Bodhisattva Vajralāsyā in the northeast corner, forming this thought:
"I am Vajralāsyā; I am now able to bestow joy and delight upon all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions."

Having formed this visualization, place the vajra-fists with palms facing upward upon both knees, close the eyes, and turn them while prostrating to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; this mudrā is named Vajralāsya (Vajra Play).
The mantra is: Oṃ vajra-rasmi. Next, one should visualize the Bodhisattva Vajramālā at the southeastern corner.
The practitioner forms this visualization:
"I am Vajramālā; I now hold these various flower garlands to make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.

Having formed this thought, he binds the vajra-fists and places them upon his forehead; then, separating the two fists, he draws them behind the crown of his head, rotating the two fists around each other twice, forming the mental image of their interlocking with each rotation.
Forming this visualization, one binds the flower garland;
this is called the Vajramālā-mudrā. Its mantra is: Oṃ vajramāle. Furthermore, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajragītā in the southwest corner.
The practitioner forms this thought:

"I am the Vajra Song; I now sing praises to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. A subtle and wondrous sound issues from my mouth, filling the infinite worlds of the ten directions."
Having formed this visualization, one should bind the vajra-fist and place it upon the mouth, gradually drawing it upward;
this is the mudrā of the melodic sound of praise. Its mantra is: Oṃ vajra-ṇṛtye. Furthermore, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajranṛtya in the northwest corner.
The practitioner forms this thought:
"I am the Vajra Dance; I perform the Vajra Dance as an offering to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions."
Having formed this thought, one binds the vajra-fist and performs a dance with both arms; this is the Vajra Dance Mudrā.
By performing this dance mudrā, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will be greatly delighted and grant all vows while protecting the practitioner’s body.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajranirutiye.

Furthermore, the practitioner arises from this gate of the Vajra Dance visualization and enters the gate of the visualization of the Bodhisattva Vajradhūpa in the northeast corner. He forms this mental image:
"I am a cloud of Vajra Incense, filling the infinite worlds of the ten directions, making offerings in the midst of space to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
Having formed this visualization, one binds the vajra-fists, placing the two fists side by side with their palms facing downward. Extending both fists, one then forms this thought:
"Immeasurable clouds of fragrance issue forth from the seal."
This is called the Vajra Incense Seal.
By forming this seal, one is able to incinerate and extinguish all afflictions, both internal and external, thereby attaining a pure mind.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajra-ruṣi-bhe. Furthermore, one enters the visualization gate of the Bodhisattva Vajrasubhūṣaṇā at the southeast corner.
The practitioner forms this thought:

"I am the Vajra-flower; I now gather all the masterless, wondrous flowers from the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
Having formed this thought, one binds the vajra-fists, placing the two fists side by side and extending them upward; this is the Vajra-flower mudrā.
What benefit is there in binding this mudrā?
In order to destroy all heavy obstructions, the mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-puṣpe svāhā. Furthermore, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajradīpa in the southwest corner.
The practitioner forms this thought:

"I am the Vajra Lamp. I now kindle an inexhaustible lamp that fills the void of immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions, making offerings to the unspeakably, unspeakably many, infinite, and boundless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
Having formed this visualization, join the two vajra fists together and bring them near the heart; this is called the Vajra Lamp Mudrā.
What benefit is gained by forming this lamp mudrā?
Manifesting the body, one accomplishes the five eyes of the Tathāgata.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajranīcī. Furthermore, visualize the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā in the northwest corner.
The practitioner forms this visualization:

"I am the Vajra-unguent. Now, this supreme white sandalwood unguent fills the infinite worlds of the ten directions within the great void of space, like a vast cloud pervading the world, making offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
Having formed this thought, he rubs his left and right necks down to his chest and abdomen with two vajra-fists, and immediately forms this thought:
"I now take this supreme ointment of gośīrṣa-candana and anoint the bodies of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and sentient beings of the ten directions."
The mantra is: Oṃ vajranīle.
Furthermore, when the practitioner arises from this samādhi, they enter the visualization gate of the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa in the true south, forming this thought: "I am Vajrāṅkuśa;
I am the great Vajrāṅkuśa of the skillful means and wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Having formed this visualization, one should form the *vajra-muṣṭi* (diamond fist) with both hands, extend the index fingers of the left and right, and slightly bend them so they hook together.

Then, extend the little fingers of the left and right and slightly bend them, bringing the two little fingers toward each other at their tips. Perform this three times to summon all the devas, spirits, and others to enter the maṇḍala.
As soon as this mudrā is formed, it enables the practitioner to attain great power, commanding all the devas and other deities to attend to various tasks.
The mantra to be recited is:

Oṃ vajra-kūṣa. Furthermore, when the practitioner arises from this samādhi, they should contemplate the visualization gate of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa in the direction of true west, forming this mental image within themselves:

"I am the Vajra Lasso; previously, I summoned all the devas and spirits, and those who had not yet arrived, I caused to enter the maṇḍala. Now, with this great Vajra Lasso, I bind them firmly so they shall not escape."

Having formed this visualization, one immediately alters the previous Vajrāṅkuśa mudrā as follows: form fists with the index, middle, and ring fingers; interlock the thumbs of both hands; and slightly bend the little fingers of both hands toward each other. This is called the "Firmly Binding All Sentient Beings" mudrā.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajrapāśa.
Furthermore, when the practitioner arises from this samādhi, they should contemplate the visualization gate of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa in the true north, forming this thought: "I am Vajrapāśa."
Having formed this visualization, one then binds the hand-mudrā.
First, interlock the tips of the left and right thumbs with the index fingers like an iron chain; the remaining fingers of both hands are then clenched into fists. This is the Vajra-Chain Mudrā.
As soon as this mudrā is formed, it enables the practitioner to properly engage in the methods of instruction and training.
The mantra to be recited is:

Oṃ vajrasphoṭa. Furthermore, when the practitioner arises from this samādhi, they should contemplate the gate of visualization for the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā in the direction directly to the east, forming this mental image within themselves:
Having formed the thought, "I am the vajra bell," one should then bind the vajra bell mudrā.
Interlace the tips of the fingers of both hands, placing the right over the left, so that they resemble the shape of a bell.
As soon as this seal is formed, one immediately gains the affection and mindfulness of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The mantra to be recited is:

"Oṃ vajragāni ṭa. At that time, after Vairocana Tathāgata had taught this secret dharma of the true seals and mudrās of the thirty-seven honored ones, he addressed Vajrapāṇi and the other Bodhisattvas, saying:

*Vajratīkṣṇe* (the second syllable *ti* is pronounced with a retroflex *ḍi*; the final syllable *kṣe* is pronounced level). Once he has held this mantra, the Ācārya takes the disciple’s hand within the maṇḍala and has him scatter various flowers. Wherever a flower falls, that is the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). The disciple should pick up this flower and practice the mantra:
"Oṃ pratisidhyeṣaṇatvami maṃ ma ha va ra. Having recited this mantra, one should immediately bind it to the crown of the deity's head."
Having placed the flower garland upon the deity, Vajrasattva shall accept the garland, and you will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
Furthermore, the *ācārya* practices the mantra for opening the eyes as follows:

*Namo bhagavate vajraśikhararājñe tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | tadyathā | oṃ cakṣuḥprativijñapaya hūṃ vāgbhava svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, he immediately opens both eyes and addresses the disciple, saying:

"Today the Great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrasattva has come of his own accord to open your eyes for you; he shall open not only your physical eyes, but also your five eyes and the supreme Vajra-eye."
"O son of good family! This is now the place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
At that time, the Vajrācārya instructs each matter within the place of enlightenment one by one, whereby he immediately obtains the empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of all Tathāgatas.
At that moment, the tutelary deity enters into one's heart; or one may see various celestial palaces, or see various lights, or see various supernormal powers.

By the power of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi will mysteriously appear before them; he will inquire about their requests and grant them according to their wishes, even bestowing upon them the Great Vajra Wisdom, the Knowledge of All Modes, and Omniscience.

Furthermore, after the Ācārya has instructed the disciple in all matters, he takes the *argha*—translated in Chinese as "the water of the full jar"—in his right hand and practices the consecration mantra. He then addresses the disciple, saying:
"Today, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi bestows upon you the most supreme consecration."
Having spoken these words, he sprinkles water upon the disciple’s head.
Immediately, the ācārya forms the vajra-añjali mudrā, places it upon the disciple’s two hands, and declares:
"All Tathāgatas have now conferred the empowerment."

Having spoken these words, the Ācārya prefixes the disciple’s name with the word "Vajra" and addresses him by that name. Placing a five-pronged vajra into the palms of both hands, he says to the disciple:
"This is the Great Wisdom Vajra of all Tathāgatas; I now hold it and bestow it upon your two hands for the sake of accomplishing the sublime siddhi."
At that time, the mantra for the yoga practitioner to practice sending the Buddhas back to their respective original lands is as follows:

Oṃ kuru te va sarvabhūta-sattva-ruṭha-siddhi-ruta-dhā ānu-ya-bhu-na-ra-ga-ma-nā-ya-ca. Once the yoga practitioner has practiced this mantra, he should ring the vajra bell three times and then loudly sing the praises of the one hundred and eight names of the sixteen Vajra Bodhisattvas, making various offerings according to his capacity.

"At that time, the practitioner shall chant the one hundred and eight names of Vajra in praise, reverently uphold the Vajrabandha mudrā with a sincere mind, and practice the mantra for dispatching all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, saying:
"Oṃ vajramayi kīśa muḥ. Having recited the mantra, one immediately releases the mudrā."
The practitioner should reflect:

"Now, this Dharma—the secret teaching briefly extracted from the ocean of great wisdom by the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana of Great Compassion—is intended solely for the benefit of those with dull faculties."
"Then, having performed this rite, the practitioner should dedicate the merit and make this vow:

'By virtue of this merit, may the first, the king; the second, my parents; the third, the donors; and the fourth, all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, all swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.'"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the great assembly, saying:

"The vast Dharma is not within my sphere; it is the sphere of the Buddha. Having now relied upon the Buddha’s great majestic spiritual power, I have briefly explained the yoga-secret true and wondrous Dharma of the realm of all Buddhas, as well as the ritual of the Great Vajradhātu Maṇḍala."

In the past, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I cultivated an ocean of vows. Thereupon, I encountered the Greatly Compassionate Tathāgata Vairocana, and within his first assembly, I heard this Dharma, transcended the eighth stage, and realized the state of Equal Enlightenment.
This secret Dharma is difficult to obtain and difficult to encounter; even if one should encounter it, it is difficult for faith to arise.
You, the great assembly, having accumulated merit and cultivated virtue over immeasurable kalpas, have now obtained this Dharma.

If one encounters this Dharma, before long one shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree upon the adamantine jewel throne, vanquish all demonic armies, shatter the shell of ignorance, dry up the river of afflictions, and forever sever birth and death; one shall realize the peerless, unsurpassed *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, give rise to the great compassionate vow for all sentient beings, and everywhere widely proclaim and disseminate it to benefit beings and cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, guiding those in the six realms of existence to realize Bodhi.
At that time, the entire assembly gathered at the ocean-like gathering, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they paid their respects and departed.
At the end of the *Buddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra* (The Sūtra on Entering the Realm of All Buddhas), Volume Lower, the colophon of the Lingyun edition states:
"On the sixteenth day of the fifth month in the third year of the Jōkyō era, this was completed with one proofreading by Jōgen at the age of forty-eight."
"Thus [he spoke]."
